text: Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous…
reflection: Peter ends a long section of practical teaching with a simple summary of how God's people should treat one another: "be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous." To be pitiful, in the old sense of the word, means to be tenderhearted. To be courteous means to be humble and kind in the way we speak and act. None of this is complicated, yet all of it is costly. It asks us to slow down, to notice how others are feeling, and to treat people like family even when they are difficult. Love is not just a warm feeling. It is a daily practice of compassion, gentleness, and respect. This month, as we reflect on love and relationships, start here. Choose one person today and treat them with intentional tenderness. A patient word, a kind gesture, or simple courtesy can become a powerful act of love.
question: Who could use your intentional tenderness and courtesy today?
prayer: Lord, make me tenderhearted and courteous. Slow me down to notice the people around me, and help me treat them with compassion and love today. Amen.

text: To Timothy, my dearly beloved son: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
reflection: When Paul wrote his final letter to Timothy, he began with deep affection: "To Timothy, my dearly beloved son: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord." Timothy was not his son by birth, but by faith. Paul had mentored him, traveled with him, and poured his life into him. Now, near the end of his own life, Paul wanted Timothy to receive the three gifts he valued most: grace for his failures, mercy for his weaknesses, and peace for his anxious heart. That is what love looks like in spiritual friendship. It does not just give advice; it blesses. It wants the very best of God for the other person. Who has been a Paul to you? And who might God be calling you to love like a Timothy? Today, speak a blessing over someone you care about. Tell them they are dearly loved, and pray that God would fill their life with grace, mercy, and peace.
question: Whom can you bless today with words of grace, mercy, and peace?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the people who have poured their lives into mine. Help me love someone the way Paul loved Timothy, and fill their life with grace, mercy, and peace. Amen.

text: Peace be to the brethren, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
reflection: Paul closes his letter to the Ephesians with a blessing: "Peace be to the brethren, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Notice where these gifts come from. Peace, love, and faith are not things we manufacture by trying harder. They flow from God Himself. We often try to build loving relationships on our own strength, and we quickly run out of patience, energy, and grace. But Paul points us to the source. When our hearts are filled with God's peace, we become peacemakers. When we receive His love, we have love to give. When faith grows in us, we can trust Him with the people we cannot fix or control. Love joined with faith is a powerful combination. It keeps loving even when the results are slow, because it trusts that God is at work. Today, before you try to love others, receive His love first. Then let it flow through you to those around you.
question: Before you try to love others today, how can you first receive God's love?
prayer: Lord, peace, love, and faith come from You, not from my own strength. Fill me with Your love first, then let it flow through me to those around me. Amen.

text: Now I beseech you, brethren, for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake, and for the love of the Spirit, that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me…
reflection: Even the great apostle Paul needed help. He wrote, "I beseech you, brethren … that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me." He was facing danger and uncertainty, and he did not pretend to be strong enough on his own. He asked his friends to pray. And notice the word strive. Prayer, for Paul, was not a casual afterthought. It was a shared effort, like teammates pulling together on the same rope. He made his request "for the love of the Spirit," because love moves us to carry each other's burdens before God. One of the most loving things you can do for someone is pray for them, faithfully and specifically. And one of the most humble things you can do is ask others to pray for you. Today, reach out to a friend and ask how you can pray for them. Then, if you are carrying something heavy, be brave enough to ask for prayer too.
question: Who can you pray for today, and what heavy thing could you ask others to pray about for you?
prayer: Lord, I cannot carry everything alone. Teach me to strive together with others in prayer, to pray faithfully for my friends, and to humbly ask for their prayers too. Amen.

text: Then said he also to him that bade him, When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee.
reflection: Jesus once looked around a dinner table and noticed who had been invited: friends, relatives, wealthy neighbors. People who could return the favor. So He said, "When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren … lest they also bid thee again." Jesus was not forbidding dinner with family. He was challenging a love that keeps score. It is easy to be generous with people who will repay us. It is far more Christlike to welcome those who never can: the lonely, the poor, the overlooked. In the next verses, Jesus promises that such kindness will be rewarded by God Himself. That changes the direction of our hearts. We stop looking to people for our reward and start looking to God. Love becomes a quiet offering to Him. Today, think of someone who rarely gets invited. Find a way to include them, and let your kindness be a prayer offered to the Father who sees.
question: Who rarely gets invited whom you could include this week?
prayer: Lord, teach me a love that does not keep score. Open my eyes to those who cannot repay me, and let my kindness to them be a quiet offering to You. Amen.

text: Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.
reflection: The man had lived among the tombs, tormented and alone. Then Jesus set him free. Overflowing with gratitude, he begged to travel with Jesus. But Jesus gave him a different calling: "Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee." Sometimes the most powerful place to share God's mercy is right at home. The people who knew this man at his worst would now see him at peace, and that change would speak louder than any sermon. You do not need a platform or a title to tell your story. You simply need to share what God has done and how He has shown you compassion. Your family, friends, and neighbors may be most moved by the quiet evidence of a changed life. Today, think about the mercy God has shown you. Then find a natural way to share it with someone close to home.
question: What great thing has the Lord done for you that you could share with someone close to home?
prayer: Lord, You have had compassion on me and done great things for me. Give me a natural way to tell the people closest to me about Your mercy. Amen.

text: And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity.
reflection: Peter describes the Christian life like a staircase, each step building on the one before. Faith leads to virtue, virtue to knowledge, and on it climbs until it reaches the top: "And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity." Charity here means love, the selfless, giving love of God. It is the crown of spiritual growth. Notice what comes just before it: brotherly kindness, the warm affection of family. Love is learned in ordinary relationships before it reaches its fullest form. You practice it at the kitchen table, in the office, in the long conversations and the small irritations. Godliness that does not lead to kindness is incomplete. The goal of all our growing is to love. If you have been focused on knowing more or doing more, pause today and ask a simple question: am I becoming more loving? Take one step up that staircase. Show warm kindness to someone close to you, and let it grow into love.
question: In what small way can you become more loving today, beginning with those closest to you?
prayer: Lord, add to my faith brotherly kindness, and to my kindness, love. Let me grow more loving, starting with the people closest to me. Amen.

text: Therefore, my brethren dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, my dearly beloved.
reflection: Listen to the affection in Paul's words: "my brethren dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown." Paul was writing from prison, yet his heart was full of love for the believers in Philippi. They were not projects or followers to him. They were family, his joy, the reward of his labor. And because he loved them, he urged them, "so stand fast in the Lord." Real love wants the people we care about to stay strong in God. It encourages them to hold on when life is shaking. Have you told the people you love how much they mean to you? Sometimes we assume they know. But words like Paul's can strengthen someone more than we realize. Today, let someone know they are dearly loved and that you are glad they are in your life. Then encourage them to stand firm in the Lord. Your words may be the very strength they need to hold on.
question: Who needs to hear today that they are dearly loved and encouraged to stand fast in the Lord?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the people who are my joy. Help me tell them they are dearly loved, and use my words to help them stand fast in You. Amen.

text: Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?
reflection: James asks a question that turns the world's values upside down: "Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?" In his day, as in ours, people often honored the wealthy and overlooked the poor. But God does not measure worth by bank accounts. Many who have little in this world are rich in faith, trusting God daily in ways the comfortable seldom need to. They are heirs of a kingdom that no market can shake. This verse is a gentle correction for anyone tempted to show favoritism. It is also a deep encouragement for anyone who feels poor, overlooked, or small. In God's eyes, you are not less. You are loved, chosen, and promised an inheritance. Today, look at people the way God does. Honor those the world overlooks. And if you are the one who feels overlooked, know that heaven sees you as rich.
question: Whom does the world overlook that you can honor as God does today?
prayer: Lord, You choose the poor of this world to be rich in faith. Help me see people the way You see them, and honor those the world passes by. Amen.

text: But thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion, and gracious, longsuffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth.
reflection: When David wrote this psalm, he was in trouble and surrounded by enemies. Yet in the middle of his distress, he lifted his eyes to who God is: "But thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion, and gracious, longsuffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth." That little word but changes everything. Circumstances were hard, but God is compassionate. People were cruel, but God is gracious. David was in need, but God is plentiful in mercy. When life feels overwhelming, remember God's character. He is not quick to give up on you. He is longsuffering, patient beyond measure. His mercy is not in short supply; it is plenteous. And because we have received such mercy, we are called to extend it. Today, rest in the compassion of God, and let it make you more patient and gracious with the people around you. The mercy you receive is meant to overflow.
question: Who around you needs the patience and mercy God has shown you?
prayer: Lord, You are full of compassion, gracious, longsuffering, and plenteous in mercy. Let Your mercy toward me overflow in patience and grace toward others today. Amen.

text: Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.
reflection: How do we know what love really is? John answers clearly: "Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us." Love is not defined by greeting cards or passing feelings. It is defined by the cross, where Jesus gave Himself completely for people who did not deserve it. And John immediately draws a conclusion: "and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren." Most of us will never be asked to die for someone. But we are asked every day to lay down our lives in smaller ways: our time, our comfort, our preferences, our pride. Love sets aside its own agenda to meet the need of another. It listens when it would rather speak. It serves when it would rather rest. That kind of love is impossible without first receiving the love of Christ. Today, let His sacrifice fill your heart. Then look for one way to lay down something of yourself for the good of someone else.
question: What could you lay down today, in time, comfort, or pride, for the good of someone else?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You laid down Your life for me. Fill my heart with that love, and show me one way to give something of myself for someone else today. Amen.

text: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering…
reflection: Paul describes a wardrobe for the people of God: "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering." The phrase bowels of mercies sounds strange today, but it means a deep, heartfelt compassion that moves you from the inside. Notice the order. Before Paul tells us what to wear, he reminds us who we are: chosen, holy, and beloved. We do not put on kindness to earn God's love. We put it on because we already have it. Like clothing, these qualities are chosen each morning. Some days, kindness fits easily. Other days, we have to deliberately reach for patience and humility. But the more we wear them, the more natural they become. Today, before you step out the door, take a moment to dress your heart. Put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Then go out into the world as one who is dearly loved.
question: Which piece of Christ's wardrobe, compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, or patience, do you most need to put on today?
prayer: Lord, I am chosen, holy, and beloved in You. Clothe my heart with mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience as I step into this day. Amen.

text: Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you.
reflection: Paul ends his second letter to the Corinthians with warm, practical counsel: "Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you." This church had been through conflict, misunderstanding, and hurt. Paul did not ignore those wounds. He called them to grow toward maturity, to encourage one another, to seek unity, and to live at peace. And then he gave them a promise: the God of love and peace would be with them. Relationships are not always easy. Families disagree, friends drift apart, and churches experience tension. But God does not leave us to sort it out alone. When we choose comfort over criticism and peace over pride, we make room for His presence. If there is a strained relationship in your life today, take one small step toward peace. Offer an encouraging word, extend grace, or simply pray for that person. The God of love and peace will meet you there.
question: What small step toward peace could you take in a strained relationship?
prayer: God of love and peace, be with me in my hardest relationships. Help me offer an encouraging word, extend grace, and take one step toward peace. Amen.

text: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
reflection: On a day when much of the world celebrates love, this verse offers a deeper kind of encouragement: "be ye stedfast, unmovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord." Love that lasts is steadfast. It shows up again and again, through ordinary days and difficult seasons. It keeps serving when no one notices. Perhaps you have been loving someone faithfully, caring for a family member, supporting a friend, serving in your church, and you wonder if it matters. This verse says it does. Nothing done for the Lord is wasted. Every patient act of love, every unseen sacrifice, every prayer is gathered up by God and given eternal value. Today, celebrate love not only with flowers or cards, but with steadfastness. Keep showing up. Keep serving. Keep loving. Your labor of love is never in vain.
question: Where are you loving faithfully without seeing results, and how can you keep showing up?
prayer: Lord, make my love steadfast and unmovable. When my labor seems unnoticed, remind me that nothing done for You is ever in vain. Amen.

text: For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
reflection: Paul makes a remarkable claim: "For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." All of God's commands about how we treat each other, honesty, faithfulness, generosity, justice, are summed up in love. If we truly loved our neighbors as ourselves, we would not lie to them, steal from them, gossip about them, or ignore their needs. Love is not a loophole that lets us skip obedience. It is the heart of obedience. It asks us to treat others with the same care, patience, and attention we naturally give ourselves. That is a high standard. We usually make excuses for our own failures but judge others harshly. Love reverses that. Today, think of someone you find difficult. Ask yourself how you would want to be treated if you were in their place. Then, with God's help, give them that same grace. That is how the whole law is fulfilled.
question: How would you want to be treated if you were in the place of someone you find difficult?
prayer: Lord, teach me to love my neighbor as myself. Give me grace toward the person I find hardest to love, and let my love fulfill Your law. Amen.

text: Knowing, brethren beloved, your election of God.
reflection: Sometimes a single sentence can hold a world of comfort. Paul writes, "Knowing, brethren beloved, your election of God." He reminds the Thessalonians of two beautiful truths at once. They are beloved, and they are chosen. They did not stumble into God's family by accident. God set His love upon them. These believers had faced persecution and hardship, and they needed to know they were not forgotten. You may need to hear the same thing today. You are not an afterthought to God. You are not loved reluctantly. He chose you, and He loves you with an everlasting love. This truth is not meant to make us proud, but secure. When you know you are chosen and beloved, you can stop striving for approval. You can face rejection without being crushed. And you can love others freely, because your own heart is already full. Today, rest in this simple truth: you are beloved, and you are chosen by God.
question: How would today change if you truly rested in being beloved and chosen by God?
prayer: Father, thank You that I am beloved and chosen by You. Let that truth steady my heart, free me from seeking approval, and help me love others freely. Amen.

text: Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour.
reflection: This proverb is painfully honest: "Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour." It describes the way the world often works. When someone has money, success, or influence, people gather around. When someone loses those things, the crowd thins out, and loneliness sets in. Proverbs does not approve of this; it simply tells the truth so that we will notice it in ourselves. Do we befriend people for what they can give us? Do we drift away when someone falls on hard times? God calls His people to be different. He is the friend of the poor, the defender of the forgotten, and He asks us to reflect His heart. The person who has lost a job, faced a crisis, or slipped into poverty needs friends who stay. Today, think of someone who may feel separated from others because of their circumstances. Reach out to them. Be the neighbor who does not leave.
question: Who may feel separated from others because of their circumstances, and how can you reach out?
prayer: Lord, keep me from befriending people for what they can give me. Help me be the neighbor who stays when others leave, and reach out to someone who feels alone. Amen.

text: And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
reflection: When asked about the greatest commandment, Jesus gave two answers that belong together. First, love God with all your heart, soul, and mind. Then He added, "And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Why is the second like the first? Because love for God naturally spills over into love for people. We cannot truly love the God we cannot see while ignoring the people we can. Every person bears His image. When we show kindness to them, we honor Him. When we mistreat them, we wound His heart. This verse invites us to see our everyday relationships as part of our worship. The way you speak to your family, treat your coworkers, or respond to a stranger is not separate from your faith. It is your faith in action. Today, let your love for God show up in how you treat the people around you. Let every kindness become an act of worship.
question: How can your love for God show up in the way you treat the people around you today?
prayer: Lord, I love You, and I want that love to spill over to every person I meet. Let each kindness I show today become an act of worship. Amen.

text: Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
reflection: Jesus spoke these words on the night before He died: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Within hours, He would do exactly that. He called His disciples friends, not servants, and then He proved His friendship on the cross. It is staggering to realize that Jesus considers you His friend. Not a distant follower, not a reluctant subject, but a friend for whom He gladly gave His life. That is the measure of His love. Nothing you face today can outweigh it. No mistake can cancel it. And because we have been loved like this, we are invited to love others with the same selfless heart. Friendship, in the way of Jesus, means showing up, sacrificing, and staying. Today, thank Him for calling you His friend. Then be that kind of friend to someone else. Love them in a way that costs you something, and you will reflect the greatest love of all.
question: How can you be a friend today in a way that costs you something?
prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for calling me Your friend and laying down Your life for me. Help me love my friends in a way that reflects Your great love. Amen.

text: Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins…
reflection: Standing in a synagogue in Antioch, Paul made an announcement that still changes lives today: "Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins." Through this man, Jesus, forgiveness is offered. Not earned, not purchased, not achieved through good behavior, but offered as a gift. Paul wanted everyone to know it. Perhaps you carry the weight of something you regret. Maybe it is a harsh word, a broken promise, or a season you wish you could erase. Hear this verse as an announcement made for you. Forgiveness is available through Jesus. You do not have to keep punishing yourself. You do not have to hide. When we receive this forgiveness, it also softens our hearts toward others. Those who know they are forgiven find it easier to forgive. Today, receive the freedom Jesus offers. Lay down your guilt, and walk out into the day as someone who has been set free.
question: What regret or guilt do you need to lay down in the forgiveness Jesus offers?
prayer: Lord Jesus, through You I am forgiven. I lay down my guilt and receive Your freedom, and I ask You to make me quick to forgive others. Amen.

text: For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed, saith the LORD that hath mercy on thee.
reflection: Mountains are the very picture of permanence. They have stood for ages, and they seem like they always will. Yet God says something astonishing: "For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed." Even if the most solid things in the world were to give way, His kindness would remain. Life can feel unsteady. Relationships change, health fails, jobs end, and plans collapse. Things we thought were permanent can shift beneath our feet. But God's kindness toward you is more stable than the ground you stand on. His covenant of peace is not fragile. It is held in place by the One "that hath mercy on thee." Today, if something in your life feels shaken, anchor your heart in His unshakable love. And let that same steady kindness shape how you treat others, especially those whose world is trembling.
question: What in your life feels shaken, and how can you anchor your heart in God's unfailing kindness?
prayer: Lord, even if the mountains depart, Your kindness will not depart from me. Anchor my heart in Your unshakable love, and make me steady and kind for others. Amen.

text: But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us…
reflection: Ephesians 2 begins with a grim description of life without God, dead in sin and far from Him. Then come two of the most hopeful words in the Bible: "But God." Paul continues, "But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us." Everything changes with those words. Our situation was hopeless, but God stepped in. And why did He do it? Not because we deserved it or earned it, but because of His great love. His mercy is rich, overflowing, more than enough for every failure. This verse reminds us that the starting point of our relationship with God is His love, not our performance. Whatever your story has been, God's mercy can write a "But God" into it. Today, think of a hard chapter in your life and remember where God stepped in. Give thanks for His great love. Then look for someone who needs to hear that their story is not over either.
question: Where in your story can you see a "But God" moment, and who needs to hear that their story is not over?
prayer: But God, You are rich in mercy, and You loved me with a great love. Thank You for stepping into my hopeless places. Help me share that hope with someone today. Amen.

text: But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?
reflection: John asks a searching question: "But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?" It is not enough to feel sorry for people in need. Real love moves us to act. John paints a picture of someone who sees a need, has the means to help, and deliberately closes their heart. That, he says, is not the love of God. This verse is not meant to burden us with guilt, but to open our eyes and hearts. Each of us has something to share: time, money, skills, a meal, a listening ear. When we notice a need and respond, God's love flows through us into the world. Today, keep your eyes open. Notice someone who needs help, and do not shut your heart. Even a small act of generosity can show that the love of God is truly alive in you.
question: What need have you noticed that you could meet today instead of shutting your heart?
prayer: Lord, keep my heart open to those in need. Let Your love dwell in me in ways that show up in real, generous action, however small. Amen.

text: And her neighbours and her cousins heard how the Lord had shewed great mercy upon her; and they rejoiced with her.
reflection: Elizabeth had waited a lifetime for a child. In her old age, God answered her prayers, and she gave birth to a son, John. Then something lovely happened: "And her neighbours and her cousins heard how the Lord had shewed great mercy upon her; and they rejoiced with her." Her joy became their joy. The whole community celebrated God's mercy together. There is a special kind of love in rejoicing with others. It is easy to weep with those who weep, but sometimes harder to celebrate when someone receives a blessing we are still waiting for. Envy can creep in quietly. Yet God calls us to share each other's joys as fully as we share each other's sorrows. Today, think of someone who has recently received good news. Celebrate with them sincerely. Send a note, say a prayer of thanks, or simply tell them how happy you are for them. Shared joy multiplies, and it honors the mercy of God.
question: Whose good news can you celebrate sincerely today?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the mercy You show to others. Free me from envy, and help me rejoice wholeheartedly with those who rejoice. Amen.

text: If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well…
reflection: James calls it the royal law: "If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well." It is royal because it comes from the King, and because it is the highest law of His kingdom. James was writing to a church that had started showing favoritism, giving the best seats to the rich and pushing the poor aside. He reminded them that love does not play favorites. It treats every person with dignity, whether they arrive in fine clothes or worn ones. We may not assign seats in church, but we can still show favoritism in quieter ways: whom we greet warmly, whom we listen to, whom we overlook. The royal law calls us higher. Today, notice how you respond to different kinds of people. Ask God to help you show the same warmth and respect to everyone, because everyone is someone He loves. When you live this way, you do well.
question: Do you treat everyone with the same warmth and respect, or do you play favorites?
prayer: Lord, my King, teach me to keep Your royal law. Help me show the same warmth and respect to everyone, because every person is someone You love. Amen.

text: For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
reflection: Freedom is one of the great gifts of the gospel. Paul writes, "For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty." Through Christ, we are free from the burden of earning God's favor, free from guilt and fear. But Paul immediately adds a caution: "only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another." Freedom is not an excuse to live for ourselves. It is an opportunity to love more freely. That is a surprising twist. The free person in Christ chooses to serve, not because they must, but because they want to. Love turns freedom outward. Think about how you are using the freedom God has given you. Is it making you more self-centered, or more generous? Today, use your freedom to serve someone. Help with a task, offer your time, or meet a practical need. You will discover that serving in love is not a loss of freedom. It is freedom at its very best.
question: How can you use your freedom in Christ to serve someone today?
prayer: Lord, You have called me to liberty. Keep me from using my freedom for myself, and teach me the joy of serving others in love. Amen.

text: Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently…
reflection: Peter calls believers to a love that is both sincere and strong: "see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently." The love he describes is unfeigned, not pretend, not polite on the outside while cold on the inside. It is pure, with no hidden motives. And it is fervent, a word that means stretched out, intense, wholehearted. This kind of love does not come naturally. Peter says it flows from souls purified by obeying the truth through the Spirit. In other words, as God changes our hearts, our love for others grows deeper and more genuine. Many of us know how to be nice. But God invites us to something richer: love that is real, warm, and persistent. As February draws to a close, ask God to purify your heart and deepen your love. Think of someone you love only halfway. Pray for them by name, and look for a way to love them sincerely and fervently today.
question: Whom do you love only halfway, and how can you love them sincerely and fervently today?
prayer: Lord, purify my heart and deepen my love. Help me love others sincerely, with no hidden motives, and with a fervent, wholehearted love. Amen.

text: The LORD is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy.
reflection: This verse is one of the most beautiful descriptions of God in all of Scripture: "The LORD is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy." Each phrase is worth savoring. He is gracious, giving us what we do not deserve. He is full of compassion, His heart moved by our pain. He is slow to anger, not quick to condemn, but patient with our failures. And He is of great mercy, holding back the judgment we might expect and offering kindness instead. This is the God who loves you. Not a harsh judge waiting for you to fail, but a gracious Father who delights to show mercy. As this month of love comes to a close, let this picture of God settle into your heart. Then reflect it to others. Be gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and full of mercy. The world desperately needs to see the love of God, and it often sees it first in His people.
question: Which part of God's character, gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, or merciful, can you reflect to someone today?
prayer: Lord, You are gracious and full of compassion, slow to anger and of great mercy. Let Your character sink into my heart and shine through me to others today. Amen.
